definition: Constant comparative analysis is an inductive research method used in grounded theory in which material from different data sources is continually compared so a theoretical framework can be developed from participants’ experiences. In this study, it meant comparing interviews, observations, and texts to identify evolving patterns and processes.

reasons: The definition states that constant comparative analysis involves “continually compared” material; the packet only says the study “utilized constant comparative analysis to inductively develop a theoretical framework” and does not explicitly describe “continually compared.”

The definition says that comparing the interviews, observations, and texts was to “identify evolving patterns and processes”; the packet specifies that multi-source data were used and that the analysis identified a set of “four interrelated stages,” but it does not explicitly mention “evolving patterns and processes.”

The remainder is broadly consistent (grounded theory approach, multi-source data including interviews/observations/textual artifacts, and developing a theoretical framework grounded in participants’ lived experiences), but the two unsupported elements above prevent a fully defensible 1–3 sentence definition.
